item.aggregated_output:
<<74:31 update 2, part 0 of 0..3>>
## THE CURRENT MAP
74:31/q01 Who are the companions of the Fire? [أَصْحَٰبَ ٱلنَّارِ · referent] (turns on: Whether the phrase denotes literal angelic guards, an elliptical construction, or allegorical human faculties.)
  74:31/q01/p1 The angels appointed to guard and administer Hell, rather than its inmates or human jailers. — reasons: Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and others connect them to the nineteen over Saqar in 74:30; Bursevī contrasts the normal sense in 59:20; Elmalılı names Mālik as chief. Al-Wāḥidī reports ḥaddād as jailer; Islahi distinguishes prison guards from inmates.
  74:31/q01/p2 The phrase elliptically means the keepers of the people of the Fire. — reasons: Kashf al-asrār supplies an omitted genitive; Bursevī rejects it because angels guard the Fire itself.
  74:31/q01/p3 The angelic powers of human perception and conception, whose misuse brings afterlife suffering. — reasons: Asad links this allegorical reading to the preceding 'over it' and to moral discrimination and ascent.
74:31/q02 Why are the Fire's keepers angels? [إِلَّا مَلَٰٓئِكَةًۭ · interpretation]
  74:31/q02/p1 Angels cannot be overpowered by the condemned, and their different nature prevents pity. — reasons: Al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, and others stress their strength, obedience, and lack of kinship. Al-Rāzī contrasts compassionate human messengers and answers that God can preserve angels from fire pain; al-Biqāʿī cites the angel's cry destroying Thamūd; 66:6 describes them as stern.
  74:31/q02/p2 Their appointment shows pure servants manage Hell as they manage the universe. — reasons: Islahi contrasts angels with jinn or devils, emphasizing exact obedience.
74:31/q03 What does their number count? [عِدَّتَهُمْ · referent] (turns on: Whether nineteen names individual chiefs, thousands, ranks, or an unspecified kind of count.)
  74:31/q03/p1 Nineteen individual angels, commonly understood as chiefs with many other angelic attendants. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī cites the majority and a report of seventy thousand reins each carried by seventy thousand angels; al-Nasafī notes Mālik as chief. The report of Abū al-ʿAwwām contrasts nineteen with nineteen thousand.
  74:31/q03/p2 Nineteen thousand keepers. — reasons: A Banū Tamīm man argues from the statement that their number is a trial; Abū al-ʿAwwām affirms the answer in Mujāhid's report.
  74:31/q03/p3 Nineteen groups or ranks of angels. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī reports an omitted classifier but considers it weak against the transmitted report and the mockery of a small number.
  74:31/q03/p4 The number may leave open whether it counts individuals or kinds. — reasons: Elmalılı says the uncertainty itself tests unbelievers.
74:31/q04 Why exactly nineteen keepers? [عِدَّتَهُمْ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the number's wisdom is inaccessible or can be derived from arithmetic, Hell's organization, or human faculties.)
  74:31/q04/p1 Its precise wisdom belongs to God's free choice and remains unknown to creatures. — reasons: Al-Rāzī compares every finite body's determinate number and every event's determinate time; al-Ālūsī prefers consigning this ambiguous matter to God and criticizes speculative rationales. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the count was chosen for an undisclosed wisdom.
  74:31/q04/p2 Nineteen combines nine, the largest single digit, and ten, the smallest greater number. — reasons: Al-Māwardī offers the possible wisdom; al-Ālūsī reports this symbolic explanation without endorsing it.
  74:31/q04/p3 The nineteen divide into six leading, six driving, six striking, and Mālik as chief. — reasons: Al-Nasafī reports this functional scheme.
  74:31/q04/p4 Nineteen corresponds to nineteen levels of Saqar or nineteen kinds of torment. — reasons: Al-Nasafī transmits both alternatives.
  74:31/q04/p5 The keepers correspond to stabilizing mountains; Hell's original number was one hundred ninety. — reasons: Al-Nasafī reports this further explanation.
  74:31/q04/p6 Nineteen is derived from schemes of levels and categories of sinners. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī records six unbeliever classes with three overseers each plus one for sinful Muslims, or five levels leaving two for major and minor sinners or men and women; the Fire was first prepared for disbelievers. He also reports twelve animal faculties and seven natural powers, and twenty-four hours less five prayer hours, judging the philosophical scheme weak.
  74:31/q04/p7 The number symbolizes causes of human corruption in an inward reading. — reasons: Bursevī's Najmī source maps nine causes of soul corruption and a hell of distance, expulsion, curse and veiling; seven prostrating limbs plus animal nature, or anger and desire, complete nineteen. Nine signifies domination and loss of mercy.
74:31/q05 What makes the number a fitna for unbelievers? [فِتْنَةًۭ لِّلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether fitna is epistemic testing through a surprising count, punitive consequence, empowered few, or a misread allegory.)
  74:31/q05/p1 The unexpectedly small number exposes unbelievers' mockery, denial, and assumption they can overpower the keepers. — reasons: Sources mention sneering at nineteen rather than twenty, its seeming inability to punish all jinn and humans, denial of resurrection, and reluctance to accept divine power. Al-Biqāʿī says the obscurity tests dispositions; Islahi compares mockery of the Night Journey and zaqqūm in 17:60; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and others gloss fitna as test.
  74:31/q05/p2 Fitna means punishment in the Hereafter. — reasons: Al-Qurṭubī compares 51:13–14; Study Quran reports the same alternative.
  74:31/q05/p3 The number is a demanding obligation through which God demonstrates that few empowered angels suffice. — reasons: Al-Jubbāʾī contrasts nineteen empowered angels with one hundred thousand strong angels; al-Aṣamm says their strength can equal a greater host; al-Naḥḥās urges recognition of God's power.
  74:31/q05/p4 The number is an allegory whose literalization misleads deniers. — reasons: Asad says the literal count distracts from the allegory; Islahi says eschatological similes describe realities known fully only to God, invoking 3:7.
  74:31/q05/p5 The trial is the disclosure of the count, not the creation of the guardians. — reasons: Al-Bayḍāwī, Bursevī, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguish announcing the number from making angels; Ibn ʿĀshūr places the trial in its mention in 74:30.
74:31/q06 How is 'we made their number only a trial' constructed? [وَمَا جَعَلْنَا عِدَّتَهُمْ إِلَّا فِتْنَةًۭ · grammar] (turns on: Whether fitna names a cause through metonymy or the condition imposed on unbelievers.)
  74:31/q06/p1 Fitna is jaʿalnā's second object and denotes the cause or occasion of a trial, with effect named for cause. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn supply an omitted 'cause'; Bursevī says the number cannot literally equal the unbelievers' temptation; al-Zamakhsharī and al-Ālūsī take the number's announcement as the effective making. Abū Ḥayyān rejects al-Zamakhsharī's substitution as unwarranted.
  74:31/q06/p2 Fitna is the condition of trial occurring to unbelievers; the restricted object names that outcome. — reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr analyzes the emptied exception in jaʿalnā's second-object slot and says the implicit point is the disclosure's trial.
74:31/q07 What incident prompted the answer that the guards are angels? [وَمَا جَعَلْنَآ أَصْحَٰبَ ٱلنَّارِ إِلَّا مَلَٰٓئِكَةًۭ · reports] (turns on: Which reported taunt and speaker elicited the verse.)
  74:31/q07/p1 Abū Jahl mocked the nineteen and challenged Quraysh to overpower the guards; a strongman offered to take seventeen while others took two. — reasons: Accounts vary the strongman's name among Abū al-Ashadd, Abū al-Ashaddayn, Abū al-Asad and al-Ḥārith ibn Kalda; some report a ten-to-one challenge, a cowhide feat, or a boast of pushing ten right and nine left. Ibn Kathīr discusses divergent wrestler identifications; Ibn Isḥāq reports later avoidance of public recitation.
  74:31/q07/p2 The verse answered an unnamed boast that even the least strong could enter Hell and then reach Paradise. — reasons: Al-Baghawī transmits this alternative preceding boast.
74:31/q08 What happened when Jews asked about Hell's keepers? [لِيَسْتَيْقِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا۟ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ · reports]
  74:31/q08/p1 They asked the Prophet or Companions the count; the Prophet indicated nineteen with his fingers and they affirmed it. — reasons: Jābir's versions vary between ten then nine and ten, ten, then nine; al-Barāʾ's version says revelation followed a Companion's deferral. Ibn al-ʿArabī calls Jābir's report authentic but notes the apparent Medinan setting; Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Ālūsī say Jews could meet Meccans or travel, and Ibn al-ʿArabī offers that Ansar had not heard the verse or did not know nineteen named keepers.
74:31/q09 Why do scripture recipients become certain? [لِيَسْتَيْقِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا۟ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether certainty arises from a matching scriptural number, divine power, or an allegorical continuity.)
  74:31/q09/p1 The Qur'anic nineteen matches their Torah or Gospel, confirming the report, Muhammad's prophethood, and revelation's divine origin. — reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and many commentators transmit the scriptural count. Al-Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ṭabrisī stress that Muhammad had not read their books; al-Rāzī adds that hearing the Messenger removes doubts about textual alteration, while proclaiming a mockable detail shows sincerity. Ibn ʿĀshūr and Islahi note certainty need not lead every informed person to faith.
  74:31/q09/p2 The count demonstrates God's power to empower one being as many. — reasons: Jishumī reports this as another account of what becomes certain.
  74:31/q09/p3 They recognize an allegory and the Qur'an's rational continuity with earlier revelation. — reasons: Asad says understanding the symbolism convinces earlier revelation recipients.
74:31/q10 Who are 'those given the Book' here? [ٱلَّذِي
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<74:31 update 2, part 1 of 0..3>>
نَ أُوتُوا۟ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ · referent] (turns on: Whether the referent is all scriptural communities, only Jews, believing recipients, or inward intellectual types.)
  74:31/q10/p1 Jews and Christians, including believing scripturalists. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī calls this most likely; al-Qurṭubī cites believers such as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām; Ibn ʿAbbās specifically understands believing recipients, while al-Qurṭubī also reports all scripturalists. Islahi describes sincere recipients who stood beside believers.
  74:31/q10/p2 Jews specifically, including those whose certainty fails to become faith. — reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr argues Jewish scholars held the knowledge and were in contact with Mecca; 2:146 describes concealed truth. He says knowledge without action becomes evidence against them.
  74:31/q10/p3 People endowed with discriminating intellect, or imitators who received scripture. — reasons: Qāshānī's inward reading contrasts intellectual certainty, direct unveiling, and unverified imitators.
74:31/q11 How does li-yastaqīna relate to 'we made'? [لِيَسْتَيْقِنَ · grammar] (turns on: The syntactic governor of the purpose clause and whether its lām denotes intention or consequence.)
  74:31/q11/p1 Its lām expresses purpose and attaches to jaʿalnā, coordinating the following faith and doubt clauses. — reasons: Al-Naḥḥās calls the lām originally prepositional, with repetition optional; Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn ʿĀshūr say it does not depend on fitna; al-Intiṣāf allows its reach across the exception; al-Rāzī also supplies an omitted 'and'. Bursevī reads the sin as seeking certainty; Ibn ʿĀshūr says istīqān intensifies certainty.
  74:31/q11/p2 It depends on an omitted 'we did this' rather than directly on jaʿalnā. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn report this alternative.
  74:31/q11/p3 The lām expresses consequence rather than an intended purpose. — reasons: Islahi takes the trial's beneficial results as consequences for sincere readers.
74:31/q12 How do believers increase in faith? [وَيَزْدَادَ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓا۟ إِيمَٰنًۭا · interpretation] (turns on: Whether faith grows by added assent and corroboration, its fruits or quality, or inward unveiling.)
  74:31/q12/p1 They affirm the newly revealed report of nineteen and gain confidence when scripture readers corroborate it. — reasons: Sources variously describe additional confirmation, assent to new revelation, witness to Muhammad's truthfulness, stronger recognition of God's wisdom and power, and more secure conviction after weighing objections. Al-Rāzī distinguishes increase in faith's fruits from essence; Ibn ʿĀshūr holds assent's quality fixed and its objects cumulative.
  74:31/q12/p2 Faith grows through unveiling and direct witnessing beyond intellectual certainty. — reasons: Qāshānī contrasts discriminating intellect, verified realization, and imitation.
74:31/q13 What does the promise of no doubt add? [وَلَا يَرْتَابَ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا۟ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ وَٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ · rhetoric]
  74:31/q13/p1 It reinforces certainty and growing faith, ensuring stable conviction about the report and prophethood. — reasons: Al-Zajjāj and al-Ṭabarī focus on the number; Jishumī adds God's power and prophethood. Al-Rāzī notes forgotten premises can reopen doubt; Abū Ḥayyān, al-Bayḍāwī, and al-Ālūsī describe settled minds despite apparent counterevidence. Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts knowledge without action among some scripture readers; al-Biqāʿī contrasts deliberate doubt.
  74:31/q13/p2 The repetition and naming of both groups prevent an ambiguous pronoun and emphasize the two distinct responses. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī says a pronoun might refer only to believers and notes the active participle's connotation of enduring faith; al-Biqāʿī says God's passive giving of scripture needs no named giver.
74:31/q14 Who have disease in their hearts? [ٱلَّذِينَ فِى قُلُوبِهِم مَّرَضٌۭ · referent] (turns on: Whether the Meccan verse predicts later hypocrisy, describes contemporary doubt or opposition, or points to Jewish envy.)
  74:31/q14/p1 Hypocrites, especially those later appearing in Medina, with doubt mingled in their hearts. — reasons: Many explain the Meccan verse as foretelling Medinan hypocrisy; al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī defend predictive revelation as miraculous. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues hypocritical motives could already exist in Mecca, invoking 29:10–11 and 22:11. Al-Rāzī also reports a broad unbeliever identification.
  74:31/q14/p2 Doubters, opponents, or wavering Meccans, not later hypocrites. — reasons: Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl invokes the Meccan setting and absence of Meccan hypocrisy; Ibn ʿĀshūr names al-Akhnas and al-Walīd and defines disease as ill intent. Muqātil instead names doubting Jews of Medina and treats the verse as Medinan. Al-Rāzī distinguishes most doubting Meccans from those sure the Prophet was false; Asad calls them half-hearted.
  74:31/q14/p3 Jealous Jews whose envy of Ishmaelites and Muhammad produces mockery. — reasons: Islahi says disease here is envy, while sincere scripturalists respond differently; Muqātil names doubting Medinan Jews.
  74:31/q14/p4 Heart disease may denote inward vices such as ignorance, cowardice and miserliness. — reasons: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports al-Rāghib's broad range but rejects extending punitive Quranic heart disease to every such trait; she limits it to hypocrisy, doubt, rancor, temptation and lust.
74:31/q15 Who are the unbelievers named beside the diseased-hearted? [وَٱلْكَٰفِرُونَ · referent] (turns on: Whether these unbelievers are Meccan polytheists or denying scripture communities.)
  74:31/q15/p1 Meccan Arab polytheists or those openly fixed in denial. — reasons: Al-Wāḥidī prefers Muqātil's Arab identification since scripture readers would not deny their own book; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Biqāʿī stress settled denial.
  74:31/q15/p2 Jews and Christians. — reasons: Al-Wāḥidī reports ʿAṭāʾ and al-Kalbī then rejects this against his Arab-polytheist reading; al-Qurṭubī reports it as the majority's view.
74:31/q16 What does the lām of 'so that they say' express? [وَلِيَقُولَ · grammar] (turns on: Whether their speech is a divine aim, an incidental consequence, or a prediction.)
  74:31/q16/p1 An eventual or unintended outcome, not the intended purpose of their objectionable speech. — reasons: The Muʿtazila, Ibn ʿĀshūr, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and others compare 28:8; al-Ālūsī distinguishes intended guidance from incidental misguidance and allows both clauses as consequence; Bursevī resolves the problem of God intending mockery this way.
  74:31/q16/p2 A real divine purpose, since God can intend their response. — reasons: Al-Rāzī says his theological position allows this; al-Ṭabrisī reports a purpose by which questioning and reflection might lead to faith. Al-Ālūsī says divine acts can be explained by purposes.
  74:31/q16/p3 A prediction of what these people will say. — reasons: Jishumī gives this beside the consequential reading.
74:31/q17 How is mādhā arāda parsed? [مَاذَآ أَرَادَ ٱللَّهُ · grammar] (turns on: Whether mādhā is a single object or mā plus a relative predicate.)
  74:31/q17/p1 Mādhā is one interrogative unit serving as the object of arāda. — reasons: Al-Naḥḥās and al-Ālūsī report this analysis.
  74:31/q17/p2 Mā is interrogative subject and dhā is a relative predicate meaning 'that which'. — reasons: Al-Naḥḥās reports dhā as 'which'; al-Ālūsī supplies an omitted relative pronoun; Ibn ʿĀshūr derives this use from the demonstrative.
74:31/q18 What is meant by 'this example'? [بِهَٰذَا مَثَلًۭا · meaning] (turns on: Whether mathal means a plain account, mockingly named extraordinary number, or genuine allegory.)
  74:31/q18/p1 It means the account or description of the nineteen keepers. — reasons: Al-Wāḥidī observes there is no explicit parable as in 2:26 and cites 13:35 and 48:29 for mathal as account; al-Layth cites 13:35, and Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 47:15. 'This' points to 74:30.
  74:31/q18/p2 They call the strange count a parable or proverb because it seems astonishing or symbolically incomplete. — reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī say nineteen rather than twenty appears defective to them; al-Rāzī says they suspect another sense is intended; al-Biqāʿī reports both astonishment and a nonliteral suspicion.
  74:31/q18/p3 It is an allegory of eschatological realities rather than a literal numerical claim. — reasons: Asad says those who literalize the count miss its purpose and compares 2:26.
74:31/q19 What do the questioners intend by asking what God wanted? [مَاذَآ أَرَادَ ٱللَّهُ بِهَٰذَا مَثَلًۭا · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the question is derisive denial or an opening to reflective belief.)
  74:31/q19/p1 They mock or deny divine authorship, asking how nineteen could frighten or punish multitudes. — reasons: Muqātil and Ibn Zayd describe skepticism at few guards; Jishumī distinguishes puzzlement from a direct numerical objection; al-Rāzī says hypocrites professed revelation outwardly while unbelievers rejected it. Al-Ālūsī and Kur'an Yolu stress the question is contemptuous, not sincere; Asad notes unbelievers would phrase it as 'your God'.
  74:31/q19/p2 Their question can initiate reflection leading to faith. — reasons: Al-Ṭabrisī reports this purposive alternative.
74:31/q20 What is the grammatical role of mathalan? [مَثَلًۭا · grammar]
  74:31/q20/p1 It is either a specification of hādhā or a circumstantial accusative from it. — reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī compares the she-camel called a sign in 11:64; al-Nasafī, al-Samīn and Bursevī transmit both; Ibn ʿĀshūr chooses the circumstantial reading.
74:31/q21 What does 'thus' point to, and how is it parsed? [كَذَٰلِكَ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the demonstrative looks back or forward; how the comparison attaches syntactically.)
  74:31/q21/p1 It points to the preceding contrasted responses of guidance and misguidance and qualifies an omitted cognate verbal noun. — reasons: Al-Naḥḥās calls the kāf an accusative adjective; al-Samīn allows a circumstantial qualifier; al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr sa

y fronting emphasizes the comparison, with Ibn ʿĀshūr rejecting comparison to 2:143. He sees the whole preceding account, not just one clause.
  74:31/q21/p2 It points forward to the following pattern. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī compares 2:143.
74:31/q22 How does God guide and misguide through this example? [يُضِلُّ ٱللَّهُ مَن يَشَآءُ وَيَهْدِى مَن يَشَآءُ · theology] (turns on: Whether God creates the response, reveals a chosen response through a test, withholds aid, judges it, or manifests primordial disposition.)
  74:31/q22/p1 God guides receptive believers and leaves mocking deniers astray according to His will and knowledge. — reasons: Al-Ṭabarī says God abandons some from truth and enables others; al-Rāzī says the verse supports his companions' doctrine and counters Muʿtazilī alternatives. Al-Nasafī attributes creation of acts to God while knowing each person's choice; Ibn ʿĀshūr grounds outcomes in created dispositions, desires, invitations and resistance, with human responsibility in 2:286. Islahi invokes God's wise law, and Kur'an Yolu stresses freely accepted or rejected guidance.
  74:31/q22/p2 The test God imposes reveals preexisting choices, so misguidance is attributed to the test's divine origin. — reasons: Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī stress obligation and manifestation rather than compelling disbelief; al-Rāzī reports a Muʿtazilī version in which verses increase faith or impurity according to response, citing 9:124–125.
  74:31/q22/p3 Misguidance means withholding divine aid, judging a person astray, or leading the condemned away from Paradise. — reasons: Al-Rāzī reports separate Muʿtazilī glosses of withholding luṭf, judging, and eschatological exclusion; Jishumī reports Abū Muslim's exclusion from reward, another judgment interpretation, and Abū ʿAlī's punishment gloss; al-Ṭabrisī reports the Paradise-path reading.
  74:31/q22/p4 God guides according to primordial felicity and misguides according to primordial wretchedness. — reasons: Qāshānī's inward account and Bursevī's pre-eternal dispositions emphasize fixed essences.
74:31/q23 What are God's junūd? [جُنُودَ رَبِّكَ · meaning] (turns on: Whether junūd embraces all divine agents, specifically Hell's angelic forces, or a philosophical scheme.)
  74:31/q23/p1 His hosts or armies: angels and other creatures executing His command. — reasons: Al-Dāmghānī gives angels here and lists other lexical senses; Bursevī includes honey among divine troops, and Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the army metaphor and the honor in 'your Lord'. Kur'an Yolu narrows the local sense to Hell's attendants.
  74:31/q23/p2 Specifically the angelic helpers behind the nineteen keepers. — reasons: ʿAṭāʾ and later sources say each chief has innumerable attendants; al-Ālūsī reports a hadith of the Fire's many reins and angels.
  74:31/q23/p3 Ten intellects and nine souls. — reasons: Ibn Kathīr rejects this Greek philosophical interpretation as unsupported and as ignoring the verse's close.
74:31/q24 What does only God knowing His hosts establish? [وَمَا يَعْلَمُ جُنُودَ رَبِّكَ إِلَّا هُوَ · interpretation]
  74:31/q24/p1 His hosts vastly exceed nineteen, and only He knows their detailed number, nature, power, roles, and wisdom. — reasons: This rebuts Abū Jahl's taunt that Muhammad's Lord had only nineteen helpers. Al-Rāzī says God can create pain directly, down to a hair or vein; al-Bayḍāwī and Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguish revealed count from unknowable total properties. Al-Ālūsī rejects al-Ṭībī's exclusive 'striking power' gloss as textually unclear. Al-Sulamī extends limited creaturely knowledge to divine names and attributes.
74:31/q25 What reports illustrate the multitude of God's angels? [جُنُودَ رَبِّكَ · reports]
  74:31/q25/p1 Heaven is densely filled with worshipping angels, with many beyond human or even Gabriel's knowledge. — reasons: Reports vary: the sky groans with no finger, palm, handspan or foot space empty; seventy thousand enter Bayt al-Maʿmūr daily without return; Ismāʿīl commands twelve thousand with twelve thousand each or seventy thousand with one hundred thousand each; Moses hears of twelve tribes innumerable as dust. Ibn Kathīr records gradings including ḥasan gharīb, strange chains, and a highly objectionable ʿUmar report, and reports other constant worshippers. Al-Ālūsī declines to affirm a ranking of hosts.
74:31/q26 How is 'none knows ... except Him' parsed? [وَمَا يَعْلَمُ جُنُودَ رَبِّكَ إِلَّا هُوَ · grammar]
  74:31/q26/p1 Huwa is the nominative subject of yaʿlam, not an accusative exception; the object is fronted for restriction. — reasons: Al-Naḥḥās gives the case argument; al-Samīn says fronting the object is required and a returning pronoun attaches to it.
74:31/q27 What does 'it' refer to in the final reminder? [وَمَا هِىَ إِلَّا ذِكْرَىٰ لِلْبَشَرِ · referent] (turns on: Which feminine antecedent the pronoun resumes: Hell, worldly fire, discourse, or the disclosed number and hosts.)
  74:31/q27/p1 Saqar or Hellfire and its description. — reasons: Al-Ṭabarī, Mujāhid, Qatāda and many others take the Fire as warning; Abū Ḥayyān prefers Saqar. Ibn ʿĀshūr says an omitted 'mention' or 'description' may be understood and notes that immediately after 74:29 the pronoun would unambiguously mean Saqar.
  74:31/q27/p2 The worldly fire, reminding people of the Fire to come. — reasons: Al-Zajjāj, Ibn ʿĪsā and others compare earthly fire with afterlife fire; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 56:71–73 and calls this semantic redirection, while al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it weakest.
  74:31/q27/p3 The Qur'anic verses, sūra, preceding address, or warning about Saqar. — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports 'the situation, address and warning'; Rāzī says only believers benefit from the ambiguous verses; Islahi prefers verses depicting Hell; Asad translates 'all this'.
